doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: His first recorded solos on 'Anthropology' and 'Yardbird Suite'
summary: He explains how he approached the solos after hearing Parker, playing fourths, and the James Moody story.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Your first two recorded solos are with that band.
On “Anthropology” and “Yardbird Suite”. When Gil did those charts had you already heard Charlie Parker’s record?
You mentioned in the book that the solo Parker played on “Yardbird Suite” had a big impact on you. How did that affect your having to play the solo on the Thornhill record?

For the most part, all of the influence that I was getting in studying these people, I tried to make it personal as quick as possible and not just review what I had learned phrase by phrase. So I just jumped in, in reaction to what the introduction, the exciting introduction that Gil had set up for me, and decided to play a lot of intervals of a fourth or something like that. Many years later I went into, this might be in the book, I went into the Sweet Basil club to hear James Moody, rest his soul, and he played one tune, and then, and I hadn’t talked to him before, he spotted me and said: “I want to tell you folks that this gentleman is responsible for my learning how to play fourths”. I said: “Wait a minute [unintelligible] he was good with fourths too.” Anyway, solos were a result of whatever anxiety I was going
through at the time. I just jumped in and that was it, I didn’t get a second chance, I don’t think, or did a second take or what.
Those [solos] made something of a name for you, early on in the game, right?
That was right. That was a sound quality I was making and fucking around with the intervals and things like that.
Obviously you were doing something right
Something like that, yeah. But I had to devote the rest of my life to straightening that out.
